planting.note: Set container-grown stock in fall into rocky, well-drained soil on an open slope or canyon rim; acorns can also be fall-sown but germinate unevenly without the warm-moist conditions of a Madrean monsoon season.

directions: Netleaf oak forms the thick-leaved evergreen canopy of Madrean encinal woodland from the Santa Catalinas and Huachucas south into the Sierra Madre, where it grows alongside Chihuahua pine and Arizona white oak on rocky slopes between about 5,000 and 8,000 feet. The leathery, net-veined leaves emerge bronze-red before hardening to dull green, giving the tree seasonal color unusual among evergreen oaks. It is remarkably drought tolerant once rooted and has been planted as a street and park tree in California precisely because it holds up through extended dry spells better than many lowland oaks. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil and avoid summer irrigation once established, since wet feet are its main cultivation hazard.

planting.note: Sow cold-stratified seed in spring into deep, gravelly pots or a nursery bed; the species pushes a long taproot early and resents being held in shallow containers before being set in its permanent rocky, well-drained site.

directions: Apache pine is one of the signature conifers of the Madrean sky islands, where its strikingly long, drooping needle bundles and sparse, open branching distinguish it from the ponderosa pines it often grows beside on mid-elevation slopes of the Chiricahuas and Santa Ritas. Young trees look almost grass-like, holding a tuft of long needles close to the ground for several years before beginning noticeable height growth, a habit that often confuses first-time growers into thinking the planting has failed. It wants full sun and coarse, fast-draining soil and is considerably less cold hardy than the Rocky Mountain pines it bridges toward, so it is best suited to warmer pockets within its hardiness range. Established trees shrug off summer drought but young seedlings need steady moisture through their first two growing seasons.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Stratify seed 30-60 days and sow in deep pots in spring, then transplant to a permanent gravelly slope while the taproot is still young; the species is unusual among pines for its ability to stump-sprout after fire, so slight root damage is more forgivable than in most conifers.

directions: Chihuahua pine mixes with silverleaf and netleaf oaks in the cooler, higher canyons of the Madrean sky islands, recognizable by slender three-needled fascicles and small cones that stay closed on the tree for over two years before shedding seed, far longer than almost any other pine. This unusual cone retention and its ability to resprout from the base after a burn make it an interesting choice for a fire-conscious Southwest conifer planting. It needs full sun, coarse rocky soil, and good drainage, and performs best where summer monsoon moisture supplements a naturally dry spring. It is slower to establish height than lowland pines, so patience is required through the first several years.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall so roots establish before summer heat; seed germinates erratically without fire-mimicking heat shock and acid scarification, so most growers start from rooted cuttings or nursery stock instead.

directions: Pointleaf manzanita forms dense evergreen thickets on the chaparral-like slopes and encinal fringes of the Madrean sky islands, where smooth mahogany-red bark and small urn-shaped flowers give it year-round interest. The tart red berries that follow the late-winter flowers are gathered locally for jam and are an important food source for birds and small mammals through the dry season. It demands sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil and resents any summer watering once established, since root rot rather than drought is its main cultivation risk. Plant it on a slope or raised bed in full sun where air and water both move away from the crown quickly.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall directly along a permanent or near-permanent water source; seed needs only light cold-moist stratification but seedlings fail quickly away from reliably moist soil, so site selection matters more than sowing technique.

directions: Arizona alder lines the perennial streams cutting through the canyons of the Madrean sky islands, forming a narrow band of shade-giving deciduous canopy that supports a distinct community of ferns and wildflowers beneath it. Smooth gray bark and small woody cone-like catkins persisting through winter make it easy to identify along a streambank even without leaves. Unlike most of its montane neighbors it has essentially no drought tolerance and needs consistently moist to wet soil, making it a poor fit anywhere but a streamside or spring-fed garden setting. Where that moisture is available it grows quickly into a graceful, multi-trunked shade tree and helps stabilize eroding banks with its spreading root system.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall into rocky, lean soil on an open slope; fresh acorns can be fall-sown directly where they are to grow since, like other oaks, this species dislikes root disturbance from later transplanting.

directions: Toumey oak is a Madrean sky-island specialty found in the Chiricahua, Huachuca, and Santa Rita ranges and adjacent Mexico, distinguished by having the smallest leaves of any native North American oak, each barely over an inch long on a dense, many-branched crown. Its naturally compact size, usually under ten feet, makes it one of the few true oaks practical for a small home garden or xeric border rather than requiring acreage. It thrives in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun and needs almost no supplemental water once its roots are established in a second or third season. Light shaping after its spring growth flush keeps the crown dense without the heavy pruning larger oaks require.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or set container plants in fall into shaded, humus-rich canyon soil; seed needs a cold-moist stratification period of several months and germinates slowly even then.

directions: Wilcox's barberry, locally known as palo amarillo for its yellow inner wood, grows in the rocky canyons and shaded slopes of the Madrean sky islands, where pinnately compound, holly-like leaflets give it a bold texture distinct from the state's more common desert shrubs. Clusters of bright yellow flowers open in spring and ripen into small blue berries by summer, both of value to pollinators and fruit-eating birds. It prefers the broken, filtered light of a canyon-bottom or north-facing slope rather than open desert sun, and appreciates somewhat richer, more humus-laden soil than most Madrean natives. Once established it is quite drought tolerant and needs little more than occasional deep watering during the hottest stretches of summer.

planting.note: Nick or hot-water-soak seed to break the hard legume coat and direct sow after the last frost, or root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer; this thorny shrub resents transplanting once its woody base has formed.

directions: Velvetpod mimosa grows along arroyos and brushy, rocky hillsides from the desert grassland up into the oak-studded foothills of the Madrean sky islands, where its fuzzy, sensitive-plant-like leaflets fold at a touch. Rounded puffball flowers in shades of pink to magenta open from early summer through fall and draw a steady stream of bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, followed by the velvety seed pods that give the plant its name. Its thorny, three-angled stems make it as useful for a barrier or wildlife hedge as for a specimen planting, and it tolerates heat, poor rocky soil, and long dry spells without complaint. Occasional pruning after flowering keeps growth dense rather than open and leggy.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in fall into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil; seed needs hot-water treatment followed by cold stratification to break dormancy and is slow and uneven even then, so most growers start from nursery stock.

directions: Desert ceanothus, long known in much of the Southwest literature under its older name Ceanothus greggii, occupies the chaparral and oak-woodland fringe of the Madrean sky islands alongside manzanita and silktassel, forming a gray, wiry-stemmed shrub armored with corky stipules. Its small white flower clusters are intensely fragrant in spring and attract a wide range of native bees, while mule deer and bighorn sheep browse the foliage through the rest of the year. It is adapted to thin, rocky, mineral soils and fails quickly in anything rich or regularly irrigated, so it belongs in the leanest, driest corner of a Southwest native garden. Avoid summer water entirely once plants are through their first year.
